query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Mo with vanadium (V) in the NbZrTiHfMo alloy will reduce the electronegativity difference that impedes dislocation mobility, thereby improving plasticity while maintaining the high compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo exists as a disordered BCC solid solution exhibiting a high compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa but limited plasticity due to the high Mo content.
generation.intervention: Replace approximately 20 atomic percent of Mo with V to form NbZrTiHf(Mo0.8V0.2).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature compression testing on as-cast samples processed under identical conditions to preserve the BCC disordered structure without additional heat treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to maintain the disordered BCC phase while reducing the overall electronegativity difference within the alloy.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the Mo content and introducing V, the electronegativity difference is lowered, which decreases bond strength heterogeneity. This promotes more uniform dislocation motion and enhanced plastic deformation, while the solid-solution strengthening effect of the constituent elements largely maintains the high yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit an increase in plastic strain (for example, an improvement in ductility by at least 5-10% relative to the base alloy) while retaining a compressive yield strength near 1700 MPa.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo with 1719 MPa compressive yield strength and limited room-temperature plasticity.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected as long as V substitution does not exceed a threshold (e.g., >20 atomic percent) that might destabilize the BCC phase or induce unwanted second phases.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal level of V substitution and the full impact on plastic deformation mechanisms remain uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys under identical conditions: the base equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy and the modified NbZrTiHf(Mo0.8V0.2) alloy. Confirm via XRD and TEM that both maintain a BCC disordered phase. Perform room-temperature compression tests to measure yield strength and plastic strain.
measurements: Total plastic strain and ductility metrics during compression
Phase analysis (XRD, TEM) to confirm BCC single phase
Chemical composition verification (e.g., EDS) and possible XPS for assessing changes in electronegativity difference
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NbZrTiHf(Mo0.8V0.2) alloy shows a significant reduction in compressive strength (greater than 10% decrease from 1719 MPa) or fails to show any improvement in plasticity, or if unintended phase segregation is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractPreviously, refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with high crystallinity were synthesized using a configurable target without heat treatment. This study builds upon prior investigations to develop nonrefractory elemental HEAs with low crystallinity using a novel target system. Different targets with various elemental compositions, i.e., Co20Cr20Ni20Mn20Mo20 (target 1), Co30Cr15Ni25Mn15Mo15 (target 2), and Co15Cr25Cu20Mn20Ni20 (target 3), are designed to modify the phase structure. The elemental composition is varied to ensure face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) phase stabilization. In target 1, the FCC and BCC phases coexist, whereas targets 2 and 3 are characterized by a single FCC phase. Thin films based on targets 1 and 2 exhibit crystalline phases followed by annealing, as indicated by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses. In contrast, target 3 yields crystalline thin films without any heat treatment. The thin-film coatings are classified based on the atomic size difference (δ).
